*Disclosure: since this is an older project and I want to move forward, this blog post was generated by AI using my original report and documentation of the project.*

**TL;DR:** This was a rasterizer project built with the aim to evoke different moods in the same scene purely through different rendering techniques. To this end, my team and I implemented bloom, fog, toon shading, normal mapping, and particle effects, all tunable at runtime. I handled the particle system (fire, smoke, and fireflies via billboards) and normal mapping; my teammates handled bloom, fog, toon shading, and building the models.

**Tech:** JavaScript, WebGL

## The Goal

The idea was simple to state and less simple to pull off: take the same scene and make it feel completely different depending on which rendering techniques are switched on. That meant every effect had to be tunable at runtime rather than baked in - bloom, fog, toon shading, normal mapping, particles, all controllable on the fly so you could actually see the mood shift happen live instead of just comparing static screenshots.

## The Journey

#### Particle System

I built a `ParticleSystem` base class managing a pool of particles with configurable lifetime, color, scale, velocity, and spawn rate, plus an `evolve(dt)` step that updates every particle each frame and a `respawn_particle()` step that recycles expired ones instead of allocating new ones. Fire and smoke are subclasses that override the evolution/respawn behavior to get their distinct physics. Particles render as camera-facing billboards - quads built from the camera's up/right vectors - handled by a dedicated billboard renderer and shader pair.

Once the billboard rendering path was solid, the fire and smoke work mostly came down to tuning evolution parameters - velocity drift, color-over-lifetime, spawn rate - rather than building new rendering infrastructure. Fireflies came along for free using the same system.

#### Normal Mapping

Added tangent/bitangent computation per vertex, averaged across all faces sharing that vertex, threaded through the vertex shader as varyings, and reconstructed into a TBN matrix in the fragment shader to transform sampled normal-map values into the correct space before feeding them into Blinn-Phong lighting.

## Final Thoughts

One limitation worth flagging: fog doesn't affect particles, since particles have no mesh or vertices for a vertex shader to operate on, and giving each particle its own mesh wasn't worth the performance cost for how many particles a scene like this needs. Something to revisit if this goes further.

Credit where it's due - **Catalina Regolf Cortes** handled toon shading and the base Blender scene, **Tizian Kurz** handled bloom and fog.
